Why Firms Exist

Coase's undergraduate essay

If markets allocate so well, why is your company not a market? Coase asked at 21.

2 min read3 figures, each sourcedWhere it is contestedCorrected onceUpdated 20 September 2026
On this pageBy the numbersHow it happenedWho did the workWhere it is contestedCorrectedWhat I changed my mind aboutGo to the sourceReads across to

Economics spent a century explaining why markets allocate resources efficiently without noticing that inside every firm, markets have been abolished and replaced by orders.

If you keep one line

Don't reorganise. Lower the cost of specifying and verifying the work, and the boundary moves itself.

ShareEmailXLinkedIn

Coase's question in 1937 is embarrassingly simple. If the price mechanism is the efficient way to coordinate production, why does anyone employ anybody? Why not contract for every task, every hour, in an open market? The answer is that using the market is not free. There are costs to discovering prices, negotiating terms, writing contracts, keeping secrets and enforcing agreements — and when those transaction costs exceed the cost of just telling someone what to do, you get a firm. The boundary of the firm sits exactly where those two costs cross.

Coase later called it “little more than an undergraduate essay”, and for decades it was little used before becoming one of the most cited papers in economics and earning him the Nobel in 1991. Oliver Williamson turned transaction costs into an operational theory of governance — why you buy some inputs and make others, especially when an asset is specific to one relationship and therefore hostage to it. Hart and Holmström then asked what a contract can and can't specify, and what happens to the residual.

The practical version is the most useful org-design tool I know. Every make-or-buy decision, every outsourcing debate, every argument about whether to hire a contractor or an employee, is a transaction-cost calculation wearing a business-strategy costume. And the answer moves: anything that lowers the cost of contracting — standardised interfaces, escrow, reputation systems, cheap search — pushes the boundary toward the market and shrinks firms.

Which is why the theory keeps predicting things. Containerisation and standardised parts lowered the cost of buying rather than making, and supply chains disaggregated across borders. Marketplaces lowered search and enforcement costs, and whole categories of employment turned into contracting. If software keeps eating the cost of specifying and monitoring work, Coase says the firm keeps shrinking — and the interesting question is which costs stubbornly refuse to fall.

01By the numbers

1937'The Nature of the Firm' published in Economica: Wikipedia, 'The Nature of the Firm'
21Coase's age on the 1931–32 Cassel travelling scholarship where he formed the question: University of Chicago Law School, 'Ronald H. Coase, Founding Scholar in Law and Economics, 1910–2013', 2013
1991Nobel awarded — 54 years after the paper: coase.org, 'Remembering Ronald Coase'

02How it happened

  1. 1931Coase, an undergraduate on a travelling scholarship, tours American factories and asks why they aren't markets.
  2. 1937'The Nature of the Firm' appears in Economica and is politely ignored.
  3. 1960Coase's 'The Problem of Social Cost' does the same trick to externalities.
  4. 1975Williamson builds transaction-cost economics into an operational theory of governance.
  5. 1991Coase receives the Nobel, more than fifty years after the essay.
  6. 2016Hart and Holmström win for contract theory — the incomplete-contracts descendant.

03Who did the work

Ronald CoaseAsked the question nobody had asked, at 21, on a study trip, and then waited fifty years.
Oliver WilliamsonTurned an insight into a method: asset specificity, hold-up, and when to bring it in-house.
Oliver Hart & Bengt HolmströmWorked out what happens when a contract can't specify everything — which is always.

04Where it is contested

Transaction costs are notoriously hard to measure, which makes the theory easy to apply after the fact and hard to test in advance. Critics argue it explains any observed boundary equally well and therefore predicts nothing — a charge Williamson's asset-specificity work was largely an attempt to answer.

05Corrected

Corrections are appended, never patched. What was wrong, and what is true now:

№ 15 · Sept 2026 · Six superlatives.

An audit of claims printed as 'first', 'only' or 'most' found six that said more than a source would. Genghis Khan's entry said he forged the largest contiguous land empire in history; it reached that size under his heirs, after his death in 1227. Rockefeller's called his the largest fortune in American history, with no measure attached; by inflation-adjusted wealth it is not, and by share of the economy it has arguably been overtaken. It now says one of the largest. Edward Thorp's said Beat the Dealer was, by his own description, the first book to prove the house edge could be beaten; his own account of the book does not say so. Why Firms Exist said Coase's paper was largely ignored for thirty years; the paper was cited long before it was put to use, and the entry now quotes only what Coase is on record as saying, that it was little more than an undergraduate essay. Maurice Hilleman's and Fritz Haber's entries stated as the house's own finding what are other people's judgments; both are now worded as such.

06What I changed my mind about

I used to think of company structure as culture and preference. It's mostly a cost calculation, and the calculation is knowable. The corollary I didn't expect: if you want a smaller org, don't reorganise — go lower the cost of specifying and verifying the work, and the boundary moves on its own.
